extracted.intended_audience: students, general readers, and practitioners interested in free speech, public discourse, and political/philosophical argument
extracted.subtask_description: Normative standards and practical principles for holding, examining, and teaching opinions in a free society — why opinions must be openly contested, how they should be tested, and what educational/political practices sustain their vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full, frequent, and fearless discussion of opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an opinion, however true, is not 'fully, frequently, and fearlessly discussed,' it will be held as a dead dogma rather than a living truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage unrestricted debate of received opinions; without open contest, beliefs calcify into rote formulas. The page emphasizes that even true opinions lose vitality if never contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons ought to learn the grounds of their opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who hold opinions on important subjects ought to be able to learn and state the grounds for those opinions and defend them against common objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivation of intellect requires knowing why one believes (not merely parroting). Teaching should aim to impart reasons and defenses, not just formulas; moral, religious, and political beliefs especially demand understanding of their grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure to opposing arguments as defended in earnest
rubrics_metrics.description: One must hear adversaries' arguments from persons who actually believe them and defend them in earnest, knowing them 'in their most plausible and persuasive form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearing only weak or caricatured versions of the other side is inadequate. Study adversaries' strongest positions (Cicero's practice) so one can feel the full force of difficulties the true view must encounter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching or imagined opponents when real ones are absent
rubrics_metrics.description: If opponents of important truths do not exist, it is indispensable to imagine them and supply them with the strongest arguments a skilled 'devil's advocate' can conjure up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where genuine dissent is rare, educators should contrive rigorous negative argumentation (Socratic dialectic or similar) to force learners to confront the most formidable objections to their beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialists answering objections cannot substitute for public airing
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough that 'somebody' can answer objections; objections must be openly stated and put in their most puzzling form so answers can be known to be satisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if experts exist to reply, the public and other intellectuals must be familiar with the objections; otherwise the adequacy of answers cannot be judged. Restricting the expression of objections prevents proper scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to write and publish is necessary for teachers and the public
rubrics_metrics.description: If teachers of mankind are to be cognizant of all they ought to know, everything must be free to be written and published without restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques restrictions (example: Catholic practice of withholding heretical books from the laity). In practice, censorship or restricted access prevents teachers and learners from encountering and resolving difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of discussion causes loss of meaning and vitality in doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Without discussion, people often forget the grounds and even the full meaning of doctrines; beliefs become mere phrases retained by rote, losing their power to guide feeling and conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with religion and everyday maxims: doctrines become external to the mind, encrusting and petrifying it; to keep doctrines alive they must be continually argued and re-understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpopular or minority opinions often contain neglected parts of the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicting doctrines frequently share truth between them; a nonconforming opinion may supply the remainder of truth omitted by the received doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value dissent even when it is one-sided or mixed with error: such views can force attention to neglected truths (example: Rousseau's criticisms exposing neglected values). Encourage expression of minority views as they can correct or supplement prevailing opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of opinion is essential for political balance
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical politics both parties of order/stability and parties of reform/progress are necessary; each derives utility from the deficiencies of the other and is kept within reason by opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On major societal antagonisms (democracy vs aristocracy, property vs equality, co-operation vs competition, liberty vs discipline, etc.), both sides must be freely expressed and defended so that neither scale dominates to the detriment of overall truth and fairness; minority opinions representing neglected interests deserve encouragement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative criticism and dialectic are indispensable intellectual disciplines
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative logic — pointing out weaknesses in theory or errors in practice — is a valuable means for attaining sound positive knowledge, especially outside mathematics and physical science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revive or retain Socratic-style dialectic and school disputations (properly grounded in reason), because they compel learners to confront opposing difficulties and thus produce deeper understanding and better thinkers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should compel acquaintance with both sides of a question
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who derives instruction only from teachers or books is under no compulsion to hear both sides; genuine knowledge requires going through the mental processes of active controversy with opponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricula and pedagogy should require students to study and fairly present opposing cases, not merely to be taught refutations; formal exercises should aim to make students understand and be able to defend or refute both sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation of opinion is inevitable but teachers must substitute contestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the gradual consolidation of opinion (many truths becoming uncontested) is inevitable and often beneficial, its attendant loss of the disciplinary advantage of contestation is a significant drawback that teachers should attempt to replace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when controversy has ceased on a question, educators should devise contrivances to keep difficulties present to learners — e.g., imagined opponents, rigorous debate formats — to preserve the vitality and understanding of accepted truths.
